faq.a: Yes; both give painless nodes, but TB often has constitutional weight loss, caseating necrosis on FNA, and responds to anti‑TB therapy.
HIV increases risk of aggressive NHL and alters chemotherapy tolerance; it also raises suspicion for opportunistic infections.
Rely on clinical pattern, B‑symptoms, and response to a short trial of steroids; refer for biopsy when possible.

exam: A 22‑year‑old with painless cervical node, night sweats, and mediastinal widening on X‑ray – what is the most likely diagnosis and why? — HL suggested by contiguous nodal spread and B‑symptoms; mediastinal mass typical.

A 45‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with a rapidly enlarging jaw mass and high LDH – which lymphoma subtype is most likely and what urgent complication must you anticipate? — Burkitt lymphoma; risk of tumour lysis syndrome requiring prophylaxis.
You have only FNA and basic IHC; how would you differentiate HL from NHL? — Look for Reed‑Sternberg morphology and CD15/CD30 positivity (HL) versus CD45 positivity (NHL).

A patient with known NHL develops sudden dyspnoea and hypotension after first chemotherapy dose – what is the likely cause and immediate management? — Tumour lysis syndrome; give aggressive IV fluids, allopurinol or rasburicase, monitor electrolytes.

In a low‑resource setting, a child presents with an abdominal mass, fever, and a peripheral smear showing ‘starry‑sky’ appearance – what is the diagnosis and next step? — Burkitt lymphoma; arrange urgent referral for chemotherapy, start hydration and uric acid‑lowering agents.
How does the presence of B‑symptoms alter staging and treatment planning? — Upstages disease to ‘B’ category, prompting more aggressive chemotherapy and closer follow‑up.
What are the key differences in nodal distribution between HL and NHL on physical exam? — HL: contiguous nodes (e.g., cervical → mediastinal); NHL: non‑contiguous, often extranodal.
Why should steroids be avoided before a diagnostic biopsy in suspected lymphoma? — Steroids can cause tumour regression, obscuring histology and leading to misdiagnosis.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Lymphoma presents with nodal and systemic signs that differ between Hodgkin and non‑Hodgkin types. Recognising pattern, age, and associated infections guides diagnosis and urgent management in low‑resource settings.

b: HL: Reed‑Sternberg cells, bimodal age peaks (15‑35, >55).
NHL: heterogeneous subtypes, more common in HIV, EBV, malaria endemic areas.
sections.p: Lymphoma is a malignant proliferation of lymphoid tissue. Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) classically shows a single contiguous nodal spread, while non‑Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) often presents with widespread, non‑contiguous nodes and extranodal disease.

b: Ann Ann Arbor stage I–IV based on nodal regions and extranodal sites.
B‑symptoms (fever > 38 °C, night sweats, weight loss > 10 %) upstage disease.
sections.p: Diagnostic criteria rely on histology, immunophenotype and clinical staging (Ann Ann Arbor). In low‑resource hospitals, fine‑needle aspiration (FNA) plus basic immunohistochemistry may be the only available tools.

t.b: Does the sample contain large atypical cells? Positive suggests lymphoma; if unavailable, rely on clinical pattern and response to empirical therapy.
Distinguishes HL (CD15+, CD30+) from most NHL (CD45+). Absence of markers limits certainty; treat as NHL if HIV/TB co‑infection present.
Detect mediastinal mass typical of HL; if unavailable, note supraclavicular node size > 2 cm as a surrogate.

b: Burkitt lymphoma: jaw or abdominal mass, high LDH, rapid growth.
HL: painless cervical node, rubbery, often with night sweats.
sections.p: Early recognition of aggressive NHL subtypes (e.g., Burkitt, diffuse large B‑cell) is vital because rapid tumour lysis can cause fatal metabolic derangements, especially where intensive care is scarce.

b: Ask about B‑symptoms and HIV status.
Palpate for contiguous vs non‑contiguous nodal groups.
Identify extranodal sites (GI, CNS, bone marrow).
sections.p: Examiners test ability to differentiate HL from NHL using history, exam and limited investigations, and to outline urgent steps when tumour lysis risk is high.

b: Assuming fever always means infection; HL often has fever.
Ignoring a solitary large node in a child – could be NHL.
sections.p: Confusing infectious lymphadenitis (TB, cat‑scratch disease) with lymphoma leads to delayed chemotherapy. Over‑reliance on normal CBC can be misleading because many lymphomas have normal counts early.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly enlarging neck or abdominal mass causing airway or bowel obstruction
New onset severe dyspnoea from mediastinal compression
Signs of tumour lysis (hyperuricaemia, renal failure) after chemotherapy start
